title: Enabling maize mapping in double-cropping regions of Argentina and Brazil without ground reference data by leveraging multiple satellite platforms
summary: Large-scale maize mapping is challenging due to the lack of field-level datasets, which were essential for training machine learning models. The United States (US) provides abundant in-situ labels and national maize maps while Argentina and Brazil offered limited data and double-cropping further complicates mapping. In this study, we propose a survey-free method for maize mapping in Argentina and Brazil, with cropping intensity considered. We first pre-trained a maize classifier on US cornfields using Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI) Relative Height (RH) metrics and Sentinel-2 imagery, then transferred this model to Argentina and Brazil to produce candidate maize labels at peak growth. We distinguished maize from other crops using phenology-based empirical thresholds. These high-confidence labels were then used to train a Random Forest model. Finally, we validated the maps with Google Street View (GSV) imagery and benchmark maps. Our framework produced 18,481 maize and 15,725 non-maize labels in Argentina and 2,125 first-season maize, 7,406 s-season maize and 7,643 non-maize in Brazil. Evaluation of our maize maps against GSV images showed satisfactory agreement, with accuracies around 90 %. The maps also aligned well with benchmark maps, exhibiting 91 % accuracy for Argentina and 88 % for Brazil. Our proposed frameworks can enhance maize mapping where field surveys are challenging.

title: SuperDove satellite detection of matter-loaded windrows with a focus on extreme environmental events
summary: Matter-loaded windrows are high-density submesoscale accumulation structures that form on the ocean surface and are often associated with extreme environmental events. This study presents a framework for windrow detection using a UNet deep-learning model applied to Planet SuperDove (PSD) 8-band satellite imagery (FLODAS). The model is trained on hand-annotated cases representing a variety of windrows and evaluated using complementary performance metrics, demonstrating consistent detection across independent scenes, while also revealing scene-specific patterns of false positives. Spectral analysis and classification based on the spectral angle distance metric is used to examine the potential for discriminating floating matter types using the PSD bands. Limited ground-truth data and the incomplete spectral characterisation of floating matter currently constrain classification performance. Application of the framework in the Aegean Sea enabled the identification of surface matter accumulations linked to storm-driven runoff and riverine discharge. The results demonstrate the potential of the framework to support in situ sampling and debris-removal operations, as well as short-term assessments of matter transport and windrow dynamics. Overall, the proposed framework represents a proof-of-concept step towards the development of operational detection systems for surface matter and marine debris accumulations.

title: A transferable framework for roof vegetation mapping across tropical cities based on open-source multimodal data and morphology-aware UDASS
summary: Green roofs play a vital role in urban sustainability, offering substantial environmental, ecological, and social benefits. However, automated roof vegetation extraction mostly relies on costly high-resolution data, with limited investigations in Global South cities. Existing methods insufficiently fuse multimodal priors and overlook domain adaptation, thereby constraining extraction accuracy and cross-regional generalization. This work presents a transferable open-source data-driven framework for cross-domain multimodal extraction and analysis of roof vegetation. Specifically, we introduce a multimodal transformer encoder to fuse Google imagery, Sentinel-2-derived products and OpenStreetMap building footprints at the feature level to improve extraction accuracy. We then propose an unsupervised domain-adaptive semantic segmentation (UDASS) model with morphology-aware pseudo-label correction to improve cross-domain generalization cost-effectively. Validated across six Southeast Asian cities, our framework achieves an F1-score of 81.71% for supervised source domain extraction and up to 70.85% for UDASS. Further validation on four additional cities spanning East Africa, South America, West Asia, and South Asia verifies its strong cross-regional generalization ability. Finally, approximately 297 ha of roof vegetation are detected across the six Southeast Asian cities, mainly on low-to-mid-rise buildings with distinct regional disparities and diverse vegetation intensity. This study delivers the first large-scale dataset on roof vegetation and green roofs for tropical Southeast Asia, establishes a cost-effective and scalable multimodal paradigm for cross-regional monitoring, and supports evidence-based green roof planning and analysis.

title: MFRXG: A multi-feature stacking ensemble RF-XGBoost model for total nitrogen retrieval in the Yellow River from Landsat 8/9 data
summary: Total nitrogen (TN) is a key indicator for assessing eutrophication in aquatic systems, and its concentration dynamics are influenced by a combination of hydrometeorological factors, terrain, and other pollution sources. However, traditional retrieval models based solely on remote sensing reflectance often suffer from limited generalization capability. This study develops a multi-feature stacked random forest (RF)-extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) algorithm (MFRXG) based on field TN data from automatic stations along the Yellow River (YR). The MFRXG integrates Landsat 8/9 satellite data, ERA5 hydrometeorological data, and terrain data to estimate the TN concentration in YR. Using an independent validation dataset in 2025, MFRXG demonstrates robust prediction accuracy and stability, with a coefficient of determination (R 2 ) of 0.75, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.53 mg/L, and a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.31 mg/L, outperforming multiple linear regression (MLR), support vector regression (SVR), artificial neural networks (ANN), RF, and XGBoost. Subsequently, the spatiotemporal changes of TN concentration in YR are investigated from 2015 to 2025. Results show that spatially, TN concentrations exhibit a fluctuating pattern with a generally increasing gradient from the upstream to the downstream of the YR. Temporally, over the past decade, TN concentrations along the main stream show an overall slight upward trend, which is primarily attributable to changes in concentration contributions from upstream areas. Overall, the proposed modeling approach provides effective technical support for long-term and dynamic monitoring of TN concentration changes in YR and fills the gaps in spatial and temporal coverage and assessment efficiency of traditional monitoring methods.

title: HeightCLIP: A vision-language network for height estimation from monocular remote sensing imagery
summary: Accurate height estimation from monocular remote sensing imagery is a fundamental task with broad applications in urban planning and management. However, existing vision-based methods rely solely on visual features, which limits their ability to fully exploit height-related semantic information. Vision-language models, e.g., CLIP, offer a promising alternative by leveraging multimodal information, yet directly adapting them to height regression remains challenging due to their weak perception of continuous numerical values. To overcome this limitation, we propose HeightCLIP , a novel vision-language framework tailored for height estimation from monocular remote sensing imagery. The task-adaptive textual prompts and image-side representations are optimized under height supervision to derive pixel-text similarity features for accurate height estimation. Specifically, we design an interval-based prompting strategy that integrates learnable context tokens and a fixed natural language template with parameterized interval values, allowing CLIP to better comprehend height-related semantics. In addition, we incorporate a reciprocal cross-attention fusion mechanism to facilitate bidirectional interaction between visual and textual features, thereby improving cross-modal feature integration. Finally, building upon this enriched feature space, we impose cross-modal consistency constraints to ensure pixel-level correspondence between height descriptions and visual features, providing more informative representations for subsequent height prediction. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets i.e., Vaihingen, Potsdam, and Data Fusion Contest 2019 (DFC2019), demonstrate that HeightCLIP achieves competitive or superior performance compared with existing state-of-the-art methods, and comprehensive ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each proposed component. The source code will be made available at https://github.com/songtaowhu/HeightCLIP .

title: Urban digital twin for environmentally sensitive mobility planning: conceptual framework and application in pilot region Leipzig
summary: This study presents the development and pilot implementation of a conceptual, practice-oriented Urban Digital Twin (UDT) used for environmentally sensitive mobility management within the pilot region of Leipzig (Germany). The UDT uses modular traffic simulations (SUMO-simulation of urban mobility), real-time sensor data and floating car data to create dynamic, near-real-time models of intermodal urban mobility systems and to evaluate mobility measures. Through a collaborative, co-production process with municipal stakeholders, the study focuses on scenario-based simulations to assess the potential impact of traffic scenarios under upcoming air pollution limits. The Leipzig case serves as a test environment for validating the technical feasibility of the conceptual UDT framework, applying a co-production process and discussing transferability of the approach. The results show the potential of UDTs to support responsive, data-driven decision-making using the developed workflow manager. In doing so, this study provides a transferable methodological basis for cities that aim at supporting urban sustainability transformations using digital twin technology.

title: DINO-Pheno-Cluster: Integrating few-shot foundation models and UAV time-series for spatiotemporal growth and functional characterization of alfalfa
summary: Precise characterization of alfalfa growth dynamics is essential for breeding accessions with superior regrowth capacity, persistence, and yield stability. However, traditional plot level and coarse scale observations suffer from low signal to noise ratios particularly before canopy closure when phenotypic data are strongly affected by weeds and soil background. Moreover, existing studies rarely capture the dynamic mechanisms of crop development across the entire growth cycle. To address this, the DINO-Pheno-Cluster framework is introduced as a foundation model driven and mechanism decomposed phenotyping approach. This decoupled framework first utilizes DINO-XMem, a few-shot individual plant segmentation network based on DINOv3 and a dual memory mechanism. It subsequently applies parameterized dynamic modeling guided by growth process knowledge. Validation utilized high frequency Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) imagery from 12 time points across three growing seasons covering 127 alfalfa accessions. DINO-XMem achieved an 89.54% mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) under a 10-shot setting and maintained 86.77% under extreme 1-shot conditions. It successfully resolved dense canopy oversegmentation outperforming fully supervised baselines by 4.08% to 11.97% in mIoU. Crucially, the extracted high purity time series trajectories were parameterized into specific biological indicators including maximum growth rate, comprehensive regeneration index, and seasonal stability index. Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) clustering based on these mechanistic traits identified four distinct functional ideotypes comprising High yield/High regrowth, Upright/Sparse, High stability/Persistent, and Short/Dense, all validated by ground measured biomass. This workflow establishes a precision screening tool for multi harvest crops advancing crop phenomics toward process level analysis.

title: PLGF-NET: A Physics-Guided Local-Global fusion network for GNSS-R high wind speed retrieval
summary: Accurate global sea surface wind speed retrieval under high-wind conditions (> 15 m/s) remains a persistent bottleneck for spaceborne Global Navigation Satellite System Reflectometry (GNSS-R). Conventional data-driven models often experience severe performance degradation in these regimes due to inherent physical limitations, including long-tail data distributions, low signal-to-noise ratios (SNR), and scattering signal saturation. To transcend these limitations, this study proposes the Physics-Guided Local-Global Fusion Network (PLGF-NET), establishing a novel physics-data dual-driven paradigm. At the data level, a Comprehensive Difficulty Score (CDS) is introduced to quantify the intrinsic physical complexity of Delay-Doppler Maps (DDMs). This metric drives a difficulty-aware hierarchical sampling strategy that rectifies long-tail biases and dynamically mines the scarce, high-wind scattering signatures. Within the network, a Physics-Guided Spatial Attention (PGSA) mechanism translates specular reflection theory into a structural inductive bias. This enforces a rigorous feature purification process, locking the receptive field onto the effective scattering window while suppressing peripheral thermal noise. Furthermore, geophysical consistency is guaranteed through a selective regularization mechanism governed by Sample Prediction Difficulty (SPD). Rather than applying uniform constraints, this approach adaptively enforces Geophysical Model Function (GMF) constraints exclusively on high-uncertainty samples, providing a robust physical anchor against signal saturation. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate the exceptional robustness of PLGF-NET. The framework achieves a state-of-the-art overall root mean square error (RMSE) of 1.38 m/s and drastically compresses the high-wind RMSE to 2.40 m/s, effectively correcting systematic negative biases. Ultimately, this scalable and physically interpretable architecture provides a highly reliable Earth observation tool for high-wind marine environment monitoring.

title: Earth Observation–Based Machine learning for operational forecasting of harmful algal blooms in the Arabian Gulf and Sea of Oman
summary: Harmful algal blooms (HABs) pose increasing risks to coastal ecosystems, fisheries, and desalination infrastructure in the Arabian Gulf and Sea of Oman. Forecasting bloom occurrence remains challenging due to strong spatial variability in physical forcing and biological response. Here, we develop a physics-informed machine-learning framework to forecast HAB probability using satellite Earth observation data and reanalysis-derived environmental predictors over the period 2002–2024. Bloom events are defined using region-specific, seasonally varying chlorophyll thresholds derived from training data, and a Random Forest classifier is used to estimate bloom probability at 8-day resolution. Operational probability thresholds are calibrated using historical data (2002–2020) and applied unchanged to independent evaluation (2021–2022) and strictly forward (2023–2024) periods. The model demonstrated moderate classification skill during the independent evaluation period (F1 = 0.46–0.67) and strong forward operational performance, achieving F1 scores of 0.79–0.97 across the study regions. Permutation importance analysis showed that chlorophyll anomaly contributed most strongly to forecast performance across regions, indicating that deviations from seasonal biomass conditions are strongly associated with bloom detection skill, while physical variables provide complementary predictive information. These findings demonstrate that a biomass-informed, Earth observation–based framework enables robust and operationally stable detection of harmful algal blooms across hydrographically complex marginal seas, supporting its application as an early-warning system for HAB monitoring and management in the Arabian Gulf and Sea of Oman.

title: Spatial heterogeneity of land subsidence in the california central valley: a model-based attribution perspective
summary: The California Central Valley (CCV), a globally important agricultural region, has long experienced severe land subsidence (LS) associated with groundwater overextraction, thereby threatening infrastructure safety and aquifer storage capacity. Although the spatial pattern of subsidence in this region is strongly heterogeneous, existing approaches still have limitations in fully quantifying the spatial variability of internal statistical associations and in systematically summarizing differentiated zones. To address this issue, this study develops the Data-Ensemble-Explanation-Cluster-Threshold (DEECT) framework, which integrates stacking-based prediction, SHAP-based explanation, clustering, and GAM-based analytical transition analysis within a single exploratory workflow. Under a conventional random split benchmark, the stacking ensemble achieved strong fit (R2 = 0.9756, RMSE = 5.3997); however, this result is interpreted only as an upper-bound reference for within-study-area exploratory analysis rather than as evidence of spatial generalizability. Under a conventional random-split setting, the stacking ensemble achieved strong fit (R² = 0.9756, RMSE = 5.3997). To assess model robustness under spatial separation, we also applied a 10 km spatial block cross-validation, under which the stacking model achieved R² = 0.9122 and RMSE = 10.1306. Compressible layer thickness, precipitation, and non-ponded agricultural pumping emerged as common high-ranking model-based attribution factors. The study area was further partitioned into four typical subsidence zones with distinct statistical association patterns, and cluster-specific nonlinear analytical transition points were identified for selected variables. Overall, the DEECT framework provides an exploratory basis for organizing within-region heterogeneity in subsidence associations and for informing subsequent zonal hydrogeological validation.

title: Dominant associations of precipitation and soil water with global vegetation reversals under climate change
summary: Satellite observations have revealed significant changes in global terrestrial vegetation over the past four decades. However, the neglect of interactions among influencing factors has sparked intense debates regarding vegetation dynamics at regional and global scales. This study systematically evaluated the spatiotemporal evolution of global vegetation dynamics (1982–2020) and their complex underlying mechanisms by integrating five remote sensing-derived vegetation products with climate and socio-economic data. The results showed that approximately 51.98% of the global terrestrial vegetation area experienced change reversals between 1995 and 2005, with vegetation “greenness” predominantly transitioning from increasing to decreasing. This percentage differs between different climate zones, ranging from 46.41% in the cold zone to 54.99% in the tropical zone. This phenomenon is associated with a weakening of the interaction explanatory power (i.e. the explained spatial variance quantified by the q-statistic) of the interactive coupling among total precipitation (TP), soil water (SW), and other factors (e.g. temperature and vapor pressure deficit, VPD), decreasing from 70% ± 4% to 64% ± 4%, rather than with an independent dominance of VPD changes, as emphasized in previous studies. These findings underscore the importance of explicitly accounting for interactions among water-related factors when interpreting regional and global vegetation dynamics under a warming climate.

title: SWOT-derived high-resolution lake surface topography for enhanced lake water level retrieval
summary: Lake water level is a fundamental variable for water-resources monitoring and hydrodynamic modeling. Although a lake surface is conventionally assumed to be flat and level, satellite altimetry measurements referenced to the ellipsoidal height system reveal an undulating surface, which renders them unsuitable for water-flux analysis and other hydrological applications. Robustly retrieving a uniform water level that conforms to a true equipotential surface therefore requires these apparent height fluctuations to be effectively removed. This study investigates the potential of the recently launched Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) satellite for lake water level retrieval. We first developed a framework integrating automatic SWOT outlier removal, geophysical correction, and multitemporal data stacking to reconstruct high-spatial-resolution lake surface topography (LST). Building on this framework, we proposed a rigorous LST correction method to improve water level retrieval from satellite altimetry. Validation against both wide-swath SWOT and nadir-looking ICESat-2 measurements demonstrates that the LST correction effectively removes surface undulations and substantially improves retrieval precision: it reduced the mean surface fluctuation magnitude of SWOT measurements from 5.04 cm to 1.50 cm and the mean standard deviation of ICESat-2-derived water levels from 4.36 cm to 2.40 cm. Relative to orthometric height, which is commonly adopted as the lake water level in standard applications, the LST-corrected water level more closely approximates a constant value. Quantitative analysis of their discrepancies shows that relying solely on orthometric height introduces an average spatial uncertainty of 6.3 cm, with local biases reaching up to 82.9 cm in extreme cases. These results confirm the critical importance of the LST correction for consistent and reliable hydrological monitoring.

title: A singularity regression kriging for spatial prediction
summary: Accurate spatial prediction remains challenging in heterogeneous environments where environmental variables exhibit nonlinear, multiscale, and non-Gaussian characteristics. Traditional kriging methods rely on simple trend models that cannot adequately capture nonlinear and multiscale spatial structures, leading to degraded prediction performance under complex conditions. This study proposes a singularity regression kriging (SRK) model that explicitly incorporates singularity-based anomaly features derived from environmental covariates into random forest trend estimation, followed by ordinary kriging of the resulting residuals. By computing covariate singularity indices at multiple spatial scales, SRK captures local multiscale heterogeneity without requiring response observations at prediction locations, ensuring robust generalisation under spatial block cross-validation. Simulation experiments demonstrate that SRK consistently improves prediction accuracy relative to ordinary kriging, with particularly significant improvements under skewed and long-tailed distributions. The SRK model is implemented in trace element (Zn and Co) mapping in a mineralised region of Western Australia and evaluated using spatial block cross-validation and parameter sensitivity analysis. Compared with common approaches, including ordinary kriging, regression-based methods, and machine-learning approaches, SRK produces more coherent spatial patterns and reduced prediction uncertainty. These results indicate that explicitly incorporating covariate singularity features into trend estimation enhances both the accuracy and reliability of spatial predictions in heterogeneous environments.

title: Integrating local spatial outliers into context-aware spatial prediction models
summary: Improving spatial prediction remains a key challenge in geographical and environmental modeling, particularly in regions with strong spatial heterogeneity. This study proposes a local-outlier-based context-aware model, named LOCA, for precipitation spatial prediction. The novelty of LOCA lies not in spatial stratification or local modeling alone, but in formalizing local outliers of explanatory variables as continuous spatial contextual predictors and integrating them with spatial stratification and stratum-specific machine-learning models. Unlike conventional approaches that mainly treat outliers as errors or noise, LOCA uses positive and negative departures from the surrounding spatial background to represent local anomaly information. The model was evaluated through a case study of precipitation prediction in Qinghai Province, China, using CRU TS precipitation data, ERA5 meteorological variables, and topographic data for 2022. Because the target precipitation product was derived from CRU TS at 0.5° resolution, this case study should be interpreted as a statistical downscaling and fine-resolution spatial prediction experiment rather than direct validation against independent 1 km precipitation observations. K-means, Gaussian mixture model, and spectral clustering were used for spatial stratification, and multiple machine-learning models were compared within different strata. Model performance was assessed using spatial block cross-validation and compared with global machine-learning models, stratified context-aware models without local outlier features, and additional spatial reference models. The best-performing configuration, GMM-based LOCA, achieved an R2 of 0.858 ± 0.125, RMSE of 77.67 ± 15.43, and MAE of 57.12 ± 14.44. The improvement was associated with two complementary mechanisms: spatial stratification enhanced regional adaptability, while local outlier-derived features provided supplementary information on local spatial contrasts. These findings suggest that explanatory-variable local outliers can provide useful contextual information for statistical downscaling and spatial prediction in heterogeneous environments.
